title: 1 Samuel 1:1–8
context: The book opens in the days of the judges, with Elkanah’s family going up yearly to worship at Shiloh, where Eli’s sons serve as priests. Hannah, loved by her husband but childless, is provoked year after year by her rival Peninnah.

verses.text: Now there was a certain man of Ramathaim Zophim, of the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
verses.arminianNotes: The story opens with Elkanah of Ramathaim Zophim, traced through his ancestors. Arminian readers note that Israel’s renewal begins quietly with an ordinary family rather than with kings or priests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God beginning a new chapter of Israel’s history in an obscure household. The genealogy roots the coming events in real people and places within the hill country of Ephraim.

verses.text: He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah has two wives; Peninnah has children, but Hannah has none. Arminian readers see the narrator honestly presenting a painful household situation without approving every arrangement in it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the tension of a divided home set out plainly. Hannah’s childlessness becomes the setting in which God will act, as with other barren women in Israel’s story such as Sarah and Rachel.

verses.text: This man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of Armies in Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests to the LORD, were there.
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah goes yearly to worship the LORD of Armies at Shiloh, where Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas serve. Arminian readers see faithful family worship set beside a priesthood about to be exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator introducing the contrast that drives chapters 1–2. The title “the LORD of Armies” appears here, stressing God’s supreme power over the circumstances that follow.

verses.text: When the day came that Elkanah sacrificed, he gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and her daughters;
verses.arminianNotes: On the day of sacrifice Elkanah gives portions to Peninnah and all her children. Arminian readers see the shared sacrificial meal, which should express joy before God, becoming an occasion of grief for Hannah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the yearly feast highlighting Hannah’s loss. The count of Peninnah’s sons and daughters makes the contrast with Hannah’s empty place at the table painfully clear.

verses.text: but he gave a double portion to Hannah, for he loved Hannah, but the LORD had shut up her womb.
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah gives Hannah a double portion because he loves her, “but the LORD had shut up her womb.” Arminian readers see God’s involvement acknowledged while Hannah’s sorrow is treated with real compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator attributing Hannah’s barrenness to the LORD. Readers in both traditions commonly see here that God’s purposes can include seasons of genuine suffering that he later turns to good.

verses.text: Her rival provoked her severely, to irritate her, because the LORD had shut up her womb.
verses.arminianNotes: Peninnah provokes Hannah severely “because the LORD had shut up her womb.” Arminian readers see human cruelty as Peninnah’s own responsibility, even though it exploits a situation God allowed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold Peninnah accountable for her taunting while affirming God’s rule over Hannah’s condition. The repetition of the phrase from verse 5 keeps God’s hand in view behind the human conflict.

verses.text: So year by year, when she went up to the LORD’s house, her rival provoked her. Therefore she wept, and didn’t eat.
verses.arminianNotes: Year after year at the LORD’s house Peninnah provokes her, and Hannah weeps and does not eat. Arminian readers see prolonged grief that is not hidden from God, even in the place of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see long, repeated suffering set before the reader. The narrative does not hurry Hannah’s pain, and it invites patience with those who grieve over unanswered longings.

verses.text: Elkanah her husband said to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? Why don’t you eat? Why is your heart grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah asks, “Hannah, why do you weep? … Am I not better to you than ten sons?” Arminian readers see a loving but limited husband who cannot fully understand or remove her sorrow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see real affection mixed with misunderstanding. Elkanah’s questions show that human love, however sincere, cannot replace what Hannah will bring directly before the LORD in prayer.
